Frontend System Design Essentials — Course: https://icodeit.thinkific.com/courses/frontend-system-design-essentials

Frontend System Design Essentials — Book: https://leanpub.com/frontend-system-design-essentials/

Have you ever worked on a frontend feature where the data is already loaded, but the UI still feels extremely slow?

The user types into a search box or changes a filter. There is no API request. But the page still freezes — the input feels delayed, and the spinner stops spinning.

Sometimes the bottleneck is not the network. It is the work the browser does after the data has already arrived.

In this video I use a log analyzer demo — 50,000 log lines (~10 MB) loaded once, then searched, filtered, aggregated, and paginated entirely on the frontend. We run the same analysis on the main thread (UI freezes) and in a Web Worker (UI stays responsive).

00:00 Data loaded — but the UI still freezes
01:27 The problem — main thread blocking
03:06 The solution — Web Workers
04:21 Basic Web Worker API
05:50 Live demo — log analyzer overview
07:38 Main thread mode — debounce is not enough
09:17 Web Worker mode comparison
10:51 Code structure — data flow and requestId
14:14 When should you use Web Workers?
14:58 Summary

You'll learn:

Why data-heavy UIs can feel slow even when no network request is happening

What the main thread is responsible for — and why long synchronous JavaScript blocks rendering and input

Why the table showing 50 rows is not where the real cost is — the full dataset scan happens first

How Web Workers move CPU-heavy work to a separate thread via postMessage

Why debounce reduces how often analysis runs — but does not make it non-blocking

The worker data flow: send large input once, send small query messages, return only what the UI needs

How requestId prevents stale worker results from overwriting newer queries

When to reach for workers vs fixing network, rendering, or memoization first
